lesson.title: Que Everywhere
lesson.subtitle: je pense que, je sais que, c'est… que — que as the master clause connector.

hook.title: que Everywhere: The Master Glue of French Thought
hook.content: Where English drops 'that' ('I think [that] it's good'), French makes que ('that') MANDATORY glue whenever one verb introduces a second clause: Je pense que..., Je sais que..., Je vois que... And C'est... qui / C'est... que acts like a vocal spotlight!

footnotes.title: How C'est… qui and C'est… que act like a spotlight
footnotes.content: C'est moi qui paie ('I'm the one paying!') and C'est demain qu'on part ('It's tomorrow that we're leaving!') spotlight any word in the sentence!

pattern.title: Never Drop que After je pense, je sais, je vois, je crois
pattern.content: Always pronounce and write que (or qu' before il/elle/on) when bridging two clauses.
pattern.linguist_note: Subordinating complementizer que is obligatorily realized in finite embedded clauses.
pattern.trap_note: Never drop que in 'I know he is here' (*Je sais il est ici) — always build the bridge: Je sais qu'il est ici!

exercises.prompt: Match each bridged clause with its English meaning:

matching_pairs.english: Je sais qu'il est là (never drop qu'!)

matching_pairs.german: You're the one who is right!

exercises.target_answer: I know (that) he is there, I think (that) it's possible, I see (that) you understand, You're the one who is right!, It's tomorrow that we're leaving!
exercises.meaning: Je sais qu'il est là (never drop qu'!), Je pense que c'est possible, Je vois que tu comprends, C'est toi qui as raison (spotlight!), C'est demain qu'on part (spotlight!)
exercises.explanation: que bridges every embedded clause and spotlights objects/adverbs after C'est.

exercises.prompt: How do you say 'I think she is ready' in French?
options: Je pense qui elle est prête
exercises.explanation: que is mandatory after Je pense, and elides before elle: Je pense qu'elle est prête!

exercises.prompt: What is the literal structure of 'C'est demain que je pars'?
exercises.meaning: Literal structure: It-is tomorrow that I leave
exercises.explanation: French uses the cleft frame C'est [X] que... to put a vocal spotlight on X.

exercises.idea: I know that it is very important
cues: I know that → Je sais que
it is very important → c'est très important
idea_parts: main verb + connector → Je sais que
exercises.target_answer: Je sais que c'est très important
exercises.meaning: I know (that) it is very important
exercises.explanation: que is mandatory between Je sais and c'est.

diagnosis.cue: Always include que after Je sais: Je sais que c'est...

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
exercises.spoken: Je pense qu'on va arriver à l'heure
exercises.target_answer: Je pense qu'on va arriver à l'heure
exercises.meaning: I think we're going to arrive on time
exercises.explanation: que elides before on: Je pense qu'on va arriver.
exercises.affirmation: You wrote qu'on with the mandatory elided que!

summary.outcome: Bridge clauses with mandatory que/qu' after verbs of knowing, thinking, and seeing, and use C'est… qui/que for emphasis.

use_example.german: Je sais qu'il est tard, mais je pense que c'est possible.
use_example.english: I know it's late, but I think it's possible.

summary.takeaway: English drops 'that'; French NEVER drops que.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next on Le Pont ([2803] Verb Dynasties: venir, tenir & prendre Matrices): see how Que Everywhere leads directly into Verb Dynasties: venir, tenir & prendre Matrices.

twist.prompt: Think it through again without looking back — express "I know (that) it is very important" in French:
twist.target_answer: Je sais que c'est très important
twist.explanation: Re-constructing "Je sais que c'est très important" from the underlying rule cements the pattern of Que Everywhere.

que.context_phrase: Paris est plus grand que Lyon.

cest.english_meaning: it is; this is; that is
cest.etymology_derivation: ce ('that') + est — the elision French performs constantly: a vowel before a vowel loses its tail.

savoir.english_meaning: to know (facts, how to do something)
savoir.etymology_derivation: Used for facts, information, and skills (je sais + infinitive, without 'how').

comprendre.etymology_derivation: To understand is literally 'to grasp together'.

vouloir.etymology_derivation: Latin volō 'I want' → vouloir. A volunteer is the one who wants to do — the want-root English kept in voluntary, benevolent.

faut.english_meaning: is necessary (il faut: one must / it is needed)
faut.context_translation: We/you have to leave now (lit. It is necessary to leave).
faut.etymology_derivation: From Latin fallere 'to be lacking' — what is lacking is what is needed! Only ever used with il.
